title: What not to put on the site for a creative studio
metaTitle: Creative studio website mistakes to cut
excerpt: Cut the unexplained reel, the vague claims, and the extra pages. Keep one decision and a way to start. A shorter truthful site beats a long performance.
alt: A person in a purple shirt typing on a bright blue laptop at a round table, editing a site down to what a client can use.
caption: Typing on a bright blue laptop at a round table. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a studio site cut first?
faqs.answer: The reel that has no sentence under it, then claims you cannot point at, then pages that repeat the offer in vaguer words. Keep one decision and a way to start a project. Length does not make a practice look more substantial.

faqs.question: Is a short site incomplete?
faqs.answer: Not if each remaining page does its job. Home, work, a few proof pages, services, about, a price shape if you can say it, and a contact path can be a complete site. A short page that ducks those jobs is a teaser, which is a different problem.

faqs.question: What should you do with pages the team worked hard on?
faqs.answer: Remove them from the navigation if they do not help a buyer start. Archive the draft. The week you spent is not recovered by making every visitor scroll through it.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
Cut the reel with no explanation. It is the most common of the creative studio website mistakes: it reassures the team and confuses a client who has already seen fifty portfolios. Keep one decision in the work and a clear way to start a project. A shorter site that tells the truth outperforms a long one that performs taste.

Those are the mistakes worth fixing first. The rest of the clutter is usually there to avoid that cut.

## The reel that explains nothing

An autoplay film of frames, grades, and hands is the most common mistake on this kind of site. It feels like proof inside the studio, because everyone remembers the projects. Outside, it is a mood. The buyer cannot point to a choice. They cannot tell what you would do with their constraint. They leave with the impression that you are busy and stylish, which is not a reason to hire you.

Replace it with one sentence and one frame. The sentence names the decision. The frame shows it. If you still want motion, put a short, silent, optional clip under the sentence, on a project page, where they have already agreed to look. Do not spend the homepage's first ten seconds on a film they cannot quote.

[Nielsen Norman Group's research](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) is the reason this is urgent and not a matter of taste. Users often leave within 10 to 20 seconds. To earn a longer visit, the value has to be clear in about 10 seconds, and people read only about a quarter of the text. A reel plus a slow headline plus a logo wall spends that budget on decoration. The quarter they might have read never gets written.

If the team mourns the reel, watch it with the sound off and write a caption for each cut. The cuts that cannot take a caption are the ones to remove. You will usually find one or two frames that were doing all the work. Keep those. Build the page around them.

## A long site that performs taste

Length is the second mistake. Extra pages make a studio feel substantial in a planning doc. On the site they create places for vague writing to hide. A journal with no point of view. A culture page. A page for every synonym of what you do. A manifesto. None of these help a client start a project. They help a team avoid choosing.

[A study of generative search visibility](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.09735) measured about a ten percent drop when pages were stuffed with repeated phrases, and it found gains when pages carried citations, quotations, and statistics. You do not need to write for a machine to use that lesson. A page that repeats "creative" in every heading is harder for a person to quote, too. One clear decision, said once, is more citable than a long performance of taste.

Keep the pages that map to jobs. Home. Work. A few proof pages. Services. About. Pricing, if you can say the shape. A contact path. That set can be complete. Add a piece of writing only when a real buyer asked a question the pages could not answer. Do not add it because the calendar said to publish.

Shorter does not mean thin. Each remaining page should carry its job in full. The homepage shows one decision and a way to start. The proof page shows the constraint. The services page gives each offer an outcome, a boundary, and a next step. A short page that ducks those jobs is not the kind of short this piece means. It is an empty state with good type.

## Claims that are not decisions

Cut claims you cannot point at. "Award-winning," with no award a buyer can look up. "Trusted by leading brands," with a logo wall that does not open. "We are passionate about craft." "Full service." "Storytellers." "A boutique with the power of a network." These lines are shared by too many sites to mean anything. They also crowd out the sentence that would have been specific.

Cut numbers you invented or borrowed. A percentage lift with no source. A client quote you polished past recognition. A headcount that flatters. A year of experience that adds up freelancers and internships into a myth. If a number is true and you may share it, put it next to the project it came from. If it is not, delete it. A quiet page is stronger than a loud one you have to defend on a call.

Cut process theater. Twelve steps with matching icons. A wheel. A pyramid. Discover, define, develop, deliver, and the rest of the alliteration. A client who has hired before knows the work is messier. Tell them the real shape in a few lines. You scope from pages and states. You design and build. You leave them with the repository and a place the files live. That is a process. The wheel was a poster.

Cut fake urgency. Limited spots. "Now booking" banners that have been up all year. Countdown timers. This buyer is skeptical of agencies. Urgency confirms the skepticism. A true note that you are booking for a later month is fine because it is a fact about capacity. A timer is not a fact. It is a costume.

## Navigation and pages that should not exist

Cut department names in the bar. Studio, lab, offerings, universe, insights. Replace them with jobs: work, services, about, start a project. A label that needs a translation is a mistake even when the page under it is good, because many people never open it.

Cut duplicate paths. Three ways to say contact. A "start a project" button and a "let's talk" button and a chat bubble. Social icons that go to accounts you do not update, placed with the same weight as the work. A search box on a ten-page site. Footer columns that repeat the header and then add every legal page as if it were a service.

Cut the password-protected portfolio as the main call to action. A locked door with "request access" is sometimes necessary for unreleased work. It is a mistake when it replaces public proof. Publish one project you can show. Keep the embargoed work for the call. A buyer should not have to apply to learn whether you can choose.

Cut a blog that exists only to chase neighboring phrases. If a post does not help a founder decide something about their site, it does not belong in the main path. Writing can be good and still be a detour. Link it from the page it supports, or leave it off the launch. A detour that ranks and disappoints is still a mistake.

## What teams keep because it feels safe

Teams keep the reel because the alternative is a sentence someone has to sign. They keep the logo wall because a thin project list makes them nervous. They keep the adjective stack because a specific sentence might be wrong, and a vague one cannot be checked. Specificity is the point. A sentence a client can disagree with is a sentence that means something.

They keep pages because someone spent a week on them. Sunk cost is not a publishing strategy. Archive the draft. Remove the nav item. The week is not recovered by making every future visitor pay for it in scrolling.

They keep stock photography of collaborators who are not them, in rooms they do not use. That is a factual error, not a style choice. Use the work, or use a true picture of the people and label it. A false studio is a strange thing to put on a site that asks for trust.

They keep motion that makes the type late. If the words arrive after a choreographed entrance, the first ten seconds belong to the choreography. Let the sentence be present. Then move, if movement helps a comparison or a state. Reduced motion should show the same content, not a broken leftover. Care here is part of the craft you are selling.

## The shorter site

A practical cut list for a weekend:

- Remove the reel from the homepage. Put one captioned decision in its place.
- Remove any claim you cannot point to in the work.
- Remove nav items that are not jobs.
- Remove fields from the contact form until only the useful ones remain.
- Remove pages that repeat another page in vaguer words.
- Read what is left on a phone. If the decision and the action are visible quickly, stop adding.

Then read the site as a stranger. You should be able to say what the studio decides, who it is for, and how to start. If you can say those three things, more pages will not increase the chance of a project. They will increase the chance of a mixed message.

Hanabi's work is a reminder that a small set of true pages can hold a practice: a heritage site, a store, a community brand, a product interface, each with a decision. You do not need a page per mood. You need a page per job. The stack under them can be ordinary and strong, Next.js and TypeScript and a site that stays fast. Ordinary and true beats elaborate and foggy.

When the cuts feel personal, that is usually a sign they are the right cuts. The team was using those blocks as a mirror. The client cannot hire a mirror.

## What remains, and what to write next

What remains is the argument. One decision on the first screen. Proof that shows the constraint. Services in the buyer's language. People with jobs. A price shape if you can say it. A contact path that explains the next week. Pictures that match the sentences. A phone layout that was designed, not shrunk.

If you want help deciding which blocks are the mirror, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). Bring the current site and the sentence you are afraid to lead with. The useful session removes pages. It does not add a new line of adjectives under the reel.

The same discipline applies when the buyer is not a client comparing portfolios, but a teacher or a parent with almost no time. [What the homepage has to prove for an education product](/blog/what-the-homepage-has-to-prove-for-an-education-product) is the next piece if that is the site you are actually building. The mistake changes shape. The standard does not. Show the thing that matters, and a way to begin, and cut the display that only comforts the team.
